Valuing A Head And Cabinet Together

A blonde Bassman head can survive in excellent condition while its original cabinet is missing. The head-only row accounts for that situation where a separate entry is available. Adding any old Fender cabinet doesn’t automatically justify the complete-set figure. The cabinet’s age, speaker configuration, covering and history need to fit the set being appraised.

Photograph the piggyback mounting hardware and any unused holes. A missing screw is a smaller issue than a cabinet modified to fit a different head, but both belong in the description. If the pieces have been together for as long as you remember, say that. Family ownership can establish a useful history without proving that Fender shipped that head and cabinet together.

Covers are easy to separate from an amp during a move. Check storage areas before selling and photograph each cover next to the piece it fits. A head cover and a cabinet cover aren’t interchangeable accessories. Torn original material may still help document the set; a modern replacement should be identified as such.

For a blackface or silverface Bassman, record the exact model name and all controls. A higher output number doesn’t by itself imply a higher collector value. The correct chart entry depends on which version you own, what accompanies it and what has changed. A head fitted into a custom combo cabinet requires an appraisal of that altered configuration.

BROAD ERAS, THEN MODEL-SPECIFIC DETAILS

Bassman Changes Across The Fender Eras
1948 To 1959: Tweed
Single Fifteen To Four Tens

The Bassman itself arrived in 1952. Fender’s history describes the TV-front 1x15, the 1953 wide-panel cabinet and the first 4x10 in 1954. Later four-input 5F6 and 5F6-A versions add the middle control. Tweed Bassman production continued into 1960, a model-specific overlap.

1959 To 1963: Blonde And Brownface
The Separate Head And Cabinet

The blonde Bassman changes to piggyback construction. The 6G6 uses a GZ34 rectifier; the 6G6-B drawing uses diodes. Rough and smooth light coverings, grille changes and early white knobs need to be checked with the dated chassis.

1963 To 1967: Blackface
AA864 And AB165 Are Different Circuits

The black-covered head loses the blonde version’s presence control and gains channel switches. AA864 and AB165 share the broad format but differ internally. A surviving earlier chart doesn’t guarantee that the chassis follows that earlier drawing.

1967 To 1980: Silverface
More Names And Higher Output

The silver-panel family includes Bassman 50, 70, 100 and 135 heads and the four-ten Bassman 10 combo. Later high-power versions use ultralinear output stages. Factory master-volume controls and rear output markings help narrow the version before a technician checks it.
